ra: Dushara is the supreme dynastic god of the Nabataeans, attested at Petra, Bostra and Hegra.
Allat is a leading Nabataean goddess, attested at Iram and across the Hawran.
Al-Uzza is the principal goddess at Petra (Temple of the Winged Lions).
Manat, as Manotu, is invoked in Nabataean tomb inscriptions at Hegra.
Hubal is named with Dushara and Manotu in the Hegra tomb-curse inscriptions.
Greek/Roman sources identify Dushara with Dionysus (interpretatio graeca).
Dushara is also identified with the sun in some Nabataean and classical evidence.
Allat is identified with armed Athena at Palmyra and Petra.
Al-Uzza is equated with Aphrodite in Greek identifications.
Nabataean tutelary god attested in dedications at Palmyra.
Protector of the qaum (people/caravan) and of warriors.
As caravan god he guards the trading companies underpinning Nabataean commerce.
Aʿra is the tutelary god of Bostra.
Aʿra is closely identified with Dushara, titled the god 'in Bostra'.
City-god of the Nabataean royal seat at Bostra.
Attested at Petra, Hegra and Sinai.
God of writing, accounting and commerce.
Nabataean scribe-and-commerce god, counterpart of Hermes/Nabu.
Invoked in the Hegra tomb inscriptions.
The Hegran cult-form of the Arabian fate-goddess Manat.
Fate-and-death goddess invoked to protect tombs and curse violators at Hegra.
As Manat 'the apportioner' she governs allotted fate.
Chief goddess of Petra.
Local Petra cult-form of the Arabian goddess al-Uzza.
The Venus goddess of the Nabataeans, identified with Aphrodite.
Idol stationed at the Kaʿba/al-Safa per Ibn al-Kalbi.
Idol stationed at the Kaʿba/al-Marwa per Ibn al-Kalbi.
Isaf and Naʾila are the petrified couple named together in the tradition.
Stationed as guardian-idols of the sanctuary precinct.
Meccan deity attested via theophoric ʿAbd Manaf.
His name ('the lofty') connotes elevated tribal status.
Major Arabian sanctuary-idol ('the Yemeni Kaʿba') per Ibn al-Kalbi.
Oracular betyl consulted by divinatory arrows.
Widely attested Arabian deity grouped among the pre-Islamic gods.
North Arabian astral deity associated with Venus, attested in Thamudic-Safaitic and Assyrian (Ruldaiu) sources.
Tribal deity of Muzayna, attested via ʿAbd Nuhm.
Sanctuary-idol of Tayyiʾ on Jabal Aja per Ibn al-Kalbi.
His sanctuary functioned as a recognised place of asylum.
Rock-idol of Banu Milkan receiving blood offerings per Ibn al-Kalbi.
His name Saʿd means 'good fortune/luck'.
Deity of the Muzdalifa hill rites near Mecca.
Storm/rainbow deity; qaws Quzaḥ ('Quzaḥ's bow' = rainbow) preserves his domain.
Named in Qurʾan 71:23; located among the Hudhayl by Ibn al-Kalbi.
Suwaʿ is listed alongside Wadd among the five antediluvian idols of Qurʾan 71:23.
Named in Qurʾan 71:23; horse-idol of Hamdan per Ibn al-Kalbi.
His name 'the preventer/protector' connotes a protective function.
Named in Qurʾan 71:23 among the antediluvian idols; the Yemeni lion-god also venerated in the Arabian sanctuaries.
Named in Qurʾan 71:23 among the antediluvian idols; the Himyaritic vulture-god also counted among the Arabian gods.
Wadd is the Minaean moon-god of the South-Arabian astral triad.
The 'Wd ʾb' amulet formula invokes Wadd as protective patron.
Qatabanian law and oracle god issuing decrees with Ḥawkam.
Anbay functioned as an oracular deity in Qataban.
National god of Hadramawt understood as a solar patron.
Sayin is the national patron of Hadramite kingship.
Hadramite moon-god bearing the lunar name Sin/Hawl.
Both are the moon-god members of their kingdoms' astral triads.
Tutelary protector of the Banu Sumʿay tribe at Riyam.
Often classed among the lunar/national gods of the Sabaean sphere.
Hawbas is regularly invoked alongside Almaqah in the Awwam cult.
Associated with fertility dedications in the Almaqah cult.
Solar 'Lady', a hypostasis of the sun-goddess Shams.
Dhat-Himyam is a solar hypostasis of Shams.
Second solar 'Lady' of the Sabaean pantheon.
The two solar Ladies are invoked as a pair.
Solar 'Lady' epithet of the South-Arabian sun-goddess.
A localized hypostasis of Shams.
South-Arabian healing god named in votive cure-texts.
Vulture/eagle deity invoked in onomastics; Qurʾan 71:23.
Deity 'he helps' named in Qurʾan 71:23 and South-Arabian theophorics.
Chief Aksumite god in Ezana's pre-Christian inscriptions.
Aksumite war god and royal patron, 'invincible to the enemy'.
Ezana's Greek inscription equates Mahrem with Ares.
Named first in Ezana's pagan triad.
Aksumite Astar is the reflex of South-Arabian ʿAthtar.
Astar is the Venus/astral member of the triad.
Second member of Ezana's pagan triad.
Aksumite god of the sea.
Greek version of Ezana's triad pairs the maritime god with Poseidon.
Third member of Ezana's pagan triad.
Geʿez medr = 'earth'; the earth god of the triad.
Functionally aligned with the Greek earth deity in the interpretatio.
Almaqah was worshipped in the Dʿmt kingdom of pre-Aksumite Ethiopia.
ʿAthtar was worshipped in Dʿmt-period Ethiopia.
Hawbas is attested among the South-Arabian gods of the Dʿmt cult.
Dhat-Himyam was worshipped in Dʿmt-period Ethiopia.
Bel was the supreme cosmic sovereign of the Palmyrene pantheon.
Yarhibol flanks Bel in the Temple of Bel as part of the Palmyrene triad.
Yarhibol is depicted with a radiate solar nimbus as the Palmyrene sun god.
Aglibol is depicted with a lunar crescent as the Palmyrene moon god.
Aglibol and Malakbel are jointly worshipped in the Palmyrene Sacred Garden.
Malakbel is a solar god equated with Sol Sanctissimus on the bilingual altar at Rome.
Malakbel ('Messenger of Bel') belongs to the circle of Bel.
Allat at Palmyra was assimilated to armed Athena and worshipped as a warrior goddess.
The Palmyrene Allat is the local cult form of the wider Arab goddess Al-Lat.
Sin of Harran is the moon god of the Ehulhul sanctuary.
The Harranian Sin is the same moon god as Mesopotamian Nanna/Sin, transmitted into the Aramean north.
Rakib-El is the dynastic protector of the royal house of Samʾal.
Rakib-El, 'charioteer of El', is a subordinate of the high god El in the Samʾal pantheon.
Sahar (Aramaic 'crescent') is a lunar deity invoked among the gods of Samʾal.
Kubaba is the tutelary protective goddess of Carchemish.
Elagabal of Emesa is the sun god worshipped as a conical betyl.
Azizos of Edessa is identified with the morning star (Venus) by Julian.
Azizos and Monimos are the paired morning/evening-star attendants of the sun at Edessa.
Monimos of Edessa is identified with the evening star (Venus) by Julian.
Khaldi heads the supreme triad as first-ranked national and war god in the Meher Kapisi list.
Teisheba is the second-ranked storm-god of the supreme triad.
Shivini is the third-ranked sun-god completing the Khaldi-Teisheba-Shivini triad.
The triad heads the Urartian state pantheon and legitimates royal sovereignty ('by the greatness of Khaldi').
At Musasir, dedications name 'Khaldi and his wife Bagmashtu'.
Bagmashtu (Musasir) and Arubani are regional variants of Khaldi's consort.
As Khaldi's consort she is associated with the feminine divine/fertility sphere.
Selardi is the Urartian lunar deity of the Meher Kapisi list.
Listed third in the female-deity sequence paralleling Shivini; taken as his consort; the capital Tushpa derives from her name.
Huba is paired with the storm-god Teisheba as his consort.
Urartian Huba corresponds to Hurrian Hepat, consort of Teshub, consistent with Teisheba being the Urartian Teshub.
Sardi is the Urartian astral/star deity; anchored to the nearest celestial-luminary abstraction.
The lance of Khaldi is the war-god's sacred weapon, credited with victory on the Karagunduz stele.
The spear is the cult weapon of Khaldi, stored in his temples as the instrument of his victories.
Cosus is a war-god of NW Hispania, equated with Mars via interpretatio romana.
Reue, from IE *dyeu-, receives primary sacrifices at Cabeço das Fraguas as a supreme/sovereign sky deity.
As an IE *dyeu-derived supreme sky-god, Reue is cognate with Zeus.
Runesocesius is analysed as a javelin/war deity.
Attested in the same São Miguel da Mota cult-complex as Endovelicus.
Thermal-spring god of the healing waters at Caldas de Vizela.
His cult centres on medicinal hot springs.
Attested at a sacred spring beside the Cávado at Braga.
The -nabiagus element links the theonym to the Nabia water-deity cluster.
A paired Lusitanian couple of the Egitania territory, sharing Trebaruna's territorial-cult milieu.
Territorial/tribal tutelary divinities of Lusitanian Egitania.
A local tutelary deity of the Lusitanian Beira region.
An indigenous Callaecian tutelary deity receiving animal offerings at Lourizán.
A specific Cretan manifestation of the Mycenaean Potnia type (KN Gg 702).
A Cretan sanctuary Potnia receiving honey offerings, associated with chthonic/earth cult.
PY Tn 316 names di-ri-mi-jo as di-wo i-je-we, 'son of Zeus'.
One reading connects qe-ra-si-ja to a beast/monster cult; a distinct Knossian deity.
A Minoan-substrate goddess of the Knossos cult lists, grouped with the Cretan Potnia-type goddesses.
do-po-ta, 'the Lord/Despotes', the masculine titular counterpart to Potnia at Pylos.
ti-ri-se-ro-e ('Thrice-Hero') on PY Tn 316, the earliest Mycenaean hero/ancestor-cult figure, chthonic in character.
i-pi-me-de-ja on PY Tn 316, a divine cult-recipient; later tradition links the name to a birth/fertility heroine.
The Thracian Horseman is repeatedly depicted hunting on votive reliefs.
Many Heros reliefs are votive dedications for healing.
The Horseman cult overlaps iconographically with chthonic/healing great gods such as Derzelas of Odessos.
Herodotus 9.119 records the Apsinthii sacrificing to the war-god Pleistoros.
A thunder-and-lightning storm god equated with Zeus/Jupiter in Roman-period inscriptions.
Inscriptions assimilate the Thracian storm-god Zibelthiurdos to Zeus/Jupiter.
Late Greek sources (Lycophron and scholia) identify the Thracian/Macedonian Kandaon with Ares.
Priese identified the Aritene of the Meroe faience medallion as a solar deity.
An indigenous Meroitic god of the Apedemak-centered Kushite pantheon.
Both are indigenous Nubian solar deities of the Napatan-Meroitic horizon.
Mash is attested only as a divine name in the Karanog inscription; wired to the head of the Meroitic pantheon.
Mash and Aritene are named together in the Karanog mortuary inscription of Haramadeye.
Dedwen is the older Nubian god absorbed into the Egyptian pantheon, aligning with the indigenous Nubian deities of Kush.
Napir is the Elamite moon god, 'the shining one', depicted with bull horns.
Napir bears the title 'protector of the gods' among the high gods headed by Humban (Hanni of Ayapir).
The Elamite lunar god, functionally aligned with the Mesopotamian moon god Nanna/Sin worshipped in Elam.
Tirutur is regularly invoked as a pair with Tepti in Neo-Elamite royal inscriptions (EKI 75).
Tirutur, like Tepti, bestows kitin (god-given royal power).
In the Hanni inscription Tirutur appears within the high pantheon headed by Humban.
Henkelman groups Suhsipa among the gods of the husa, a funerary/netherworld sphere.
Suhsipa is grouped with Simut and Manzat among the husa-related deities.
Suhsipa had a temple at Dur-Untash alongside Lagamar and Napirisha.
